overall.sentence: Circular-polarization Raman intensity differences in a centrosymmetric ferroaxial phase were already reported in 1T-TaS2, which the paper cites; what is new is a large, resonance-enhanced ROA in a bulk insulating ferroaxial crystal with independently known domains, tied to the sign of the axial vector and backed by a microscopic electric-dipole model.

assessment.claim: 1: ROA arises in a centrosymmetric, non-magnetic ferroaxial crystal (abstract: 'Here we demonstrate that ROA can also arise...')
assessment.note: Same question and method in a centrosymmetric ferroaxial (chiral CDW, point group -3) phase of 1T-TaS2, cited as [3]-[6]; new here is the system, a bulk ilmenite insulator with structural ferroaxial order and g_ROA near 1.

assessment.claim: 2: the sign of g_ROA follows the orientation of the ferroaxial vector (front/back reversal)
assessment.note: NiCo2TeO6 [7] already showed complete Raman circular dichroism whose sign is set by C.P = A; new here is a centrosymmetric host where A is the only order parameter.

assessment.claim: 5: the microscopic mechanism of ferroaxial NROA was unknown; symmetry and tight-binding show it arises from ferroaxial order within the electric dipole approximation
assessment.note: 1T-TaS2 work [4] already explained its ROA by complex Raman tensors from absorption (also electric dipole); the symmetry-adapted model linking the imbalance |R1| != |R2| to ferroaxial orbital rotation found no earlier match in these searches.

assessment.claim: 6: Raman ROA mapping images ferroaxial domains
assessment.note: Ferroaxial domains in NiTiO3 were already imaged by SHG microscopy [17] and electrogyration [15],[23]; new is the method, circularly polarized Raman.

positioning: The paper sits between the 1T-TaS2 chiral-CDW Raman work (centrosymmetric, ferroaxial, but electronic order in a metal and attributed to absorption-induced complex Raman tensors) and NiCo2TeO6 (ferroaxial Raman circular dichroism, but in a chiral and polar crystal); both are cited and discussed in the introduction. What it adds, as far as these searches show, is a large ROA in a centrosymmetric bulk insulator whose ferroaxial domains are known independently, its sign tied to the axial vector, its resonance with the Ni d-d band, and a symmetry-adapted microscopic model. The only item worth raising is that the abstract frames ROA in centrosymmetric ferroaxial systems as wholly new while the introduction acknowledges the 1T-TaS2 precedent; several closely related papers (Na2BaNi(PO4)2, FeS2, Ni3TeO6, axial-phonon circular dichroism) were posted after this paper and are context only.

issues.claim: ROA arises in a centrosymmetric, non-magnetic ferroaxial crystal
issues.headline: Abstract presents centrosymmetric ferroaxial ROA as new despite 1T-TaS2
issues.issue: The abstract contrasts NiTiO3 only with chiral molecules and magnetic materials, but the introduction itself cites circular Raman intensity differences in the centrosymmetric, ferroaxial chiral-CDW phase of 1T-TaS2 (Yang et al., arXiv:2205.09600, ref. [4], and refs. [3],[5],[6]). A referee who knows that work will read the abstract as overstating priority; naming the first bulk, structurally ferroaxial insulator is accurate and still strong.

evidence.quote: Here we demonstrate that ROA can also arise in a centrosymmetric and non-magnetic ferroaxial crystal.

issues.fix: Acknowledge the 1T-TaS2 observations in the abstract and state the contribution as a large ROA in a bulk ferroaxial insulator whose sign tracks the ferroaxial vector, with a microscopic mechanism.

edit.before: Here we demonstrate that ROA can also arise in a centrosymmetric and non-magnetic ferroaxial crystal.
edit.after: Building on reports of circular Raman intensity differences in the chiral charge-density-wave phase of 1T-TaS2, here we demonstrate that a large ROA arises in a centrosymmetric, non-magnetic bulk crystal with structural ferroaxial order.

issues.claim: ROA as a probe of ferroaxial order in centrosymmetric systems
issues.headline: Uncited Raman probe of ferroaxial order in centrosymmetric RTe3
issues.issue: The abstract presents Raman (via ROA) as a new probe of ferroaxial order in centrosymmetric systems, but Singh et al. (arXiv:2411.08322) already used Raman scattering, through an axial Higgs mode, to identify a ferroaxial phase in centrosymmetric RTe3. The paper does not cite this line of work; one sentence positioning ROA against it would pre-empt the comparison.

evidence.quote: These results establish ROA as a powerful probe of ferroaxial order in centrosymmetric systems.

issues.fix: Cite the RTe3 axial Higgs work in the introduction as an earlier Raman signature of ferroaxial order, and state what ROA adds: sensitivity to the sign of the axial vector and hence domain imaging.
